title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6655 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

Christine Lagarde is leaving early. She steps down on February 7, nine months before her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027. The timing is political. Leaving early lets EU leaders lock in a successor before April's French presidential election, where polls favour Marine Le Pen (and will be a major event in FX markets next year). The race was really decided when Paris and Berlin agreed on a deal. France backed De Cos for the top job and proposed a Frenchwoman for the market operations role. title: Connecting the dots: Is big tech starting to outgrow its own valuation playbook?

Or at least that used to be how it used to be. Historically, the appeal of software and digital platforms has always been their ability to scale. Selling another million software subscriptions doesn't necessarily require building another factory. As such, revenues can grow much faster than the cost of doing business. And that is part of the reason Wall Street has been so comfortable attaching lofty valuations to tech stocks. However, the AI trade is a completely different beast. Between the need for data centres, expensive chips, electricity and networking infrastructure, growth is becoming a much more expensive affair. And as investors are grappling with the latest selloff in tech stocks, perhaps we should be asking how big of an issue is the changing economics of the tech business itself? Let's try to put things into perspective. According to a research published by Brookings, the combined capex by Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle is projected to exceed $800 billion this year. title: What really drives the FX market? A look at interest rate differentials
body: The FX market is highly sensitive to interest rates. This is one of the most important concepts to understand when trading currencies. In fact, interest rate differentials are the main drivers of major currencies. The reason for this relationship is pretty simple: higher interest rates tend to attract foreign investment, increasing the demand and value of the currency. On the other hand, lower interest rates tend to be less attractive for foreign investment and decrease the currency's value. Therefore, monetary policy divergence (or better yet divergence in interest rate expectations) between two countries is the key driver. Emerging market currencies are generally driven by changes in the US dollar and certain commodities due to the impact they have on their economies and the perceived risk from investors. You are unlikely to be trading those since they have wider spreads, higher costs, increased risks and generally have limited availability with retail brokers. Now, imagine that US interest rates are significantly higher than euro-area interest rates. An investor deciding where to allocate capital may find US assets more attractive because they offer a higher yield. To purchase those US assets, the investor generally needs US dollars. This creates demand for USD. This is one reason why interest-rate differentials are so important in FX.

The proposal could improve the network's long-term funding structure, but it also introduces uncertainty around how development will be financed. Looking ahead, Zcash remains exposed to the same macro headwinds as the broader crypto market, and further downside cannot be ruled out if risk-off conditions persist.

title: Macro pulse: Is the Santa Claus rally losing its magic on Wall Street?
body: The trouble with market traditions is that we sometimes forget to ask whether they still work. With December just around the corner, you can expect to hear plenty of chatter about the Santa Claus rally coming to town in the weeks ahead. And after the rather miserable November we've had in Wall Street, investors will be surely hoping for a bit more of a Christmas cheer to wrap up the year. But before we get too carried away with the festive spirit, let's revisit the whole concept of the Santa Claus rally. The thing that we should really be asking is whether it is still as useful a seasonal trading tool as it once was. For those unfamiliar with the phenomenon, it typically refers to the tendency for US stocks to rise during the final five trading days of December and the first two of January. And there's good reason why it has earned a place in Wall Street's trading calendar. According to LPL Research, the S&P 500 has historically averaged a gain of 1.3% during this window as compared to just 0.3% during a typical seven-day trading period. Taken at face value, there is certainly the temptation to trade on those numbers alone. However, let's take a step back and remind ourselves that markets of today definitely do not behave like markets of yesteryear. After all, that research figure is one that dates back to 1950. Talk about the stone age for markets, eh? And when we break down the numbers a little further, we get a rather different picture.

title: Month-end FX rebalancing signals favour the dollar - Credit Agricole
body: As if the dollar needed another excuse to stay bid this month. As November trading draws toward a close, we're getting to that time of the month when portfolio rebalancing flows can throw a little spanner in the works for FX traders. This time around, Credit Agricole's month-end fixing model is pointing to moderate dollar buying across the board, with the strongest buy signal coming against the Swedish krona. The firm notes that: "Global equity markets were lower across the board in November. In FX, the USD has outperformed across the board on the month. Overall, the moves in equity markets, when adjusted for market capitalisation and FX performance this month, suggest month-end portfolio-rebalancing flows are likely to be moderate USD buying across the board with the strongest buy signal in the case of the USD vs SEK." For the uninitiated, think of these flows as a bit of housekeeping being done by large fund managers. As the value of their investments changes throughout the month, they may need to buy or sell currencies to bring their portfolio allocations and currency hedges back in line by the end of it. As such, these flows aren't necessarily a reflection of what the general market backdrop or conviction is playing out to be. The added complication for November though is that there is also the Thanksgiving holiday thinning out liquidity today and tomorrow.

title: China hits back at Trump's latest tariff threat as trade war tensions resurface
body: It looks like a trade war is back on the menu again. Just when markets thought they could afford to spend a little less time worrying about US-China tensions, we're back to the familiar exchange of threats between Washington and Beijing this week. China's commerce ministry is hitting back at the latest US tariff proposals today, expressing firm opposition to Washington's Section 301 investigation into structural overcapacity. "China urges the US to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation. China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests." As a reminder, the US is proposing additional tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners and that includes a 20% tariff on Chinese goods. In doing so, the latest proposal would bring the average effective tariff rate on Chinese goods back up to roughly 31%. In essence, US president Trump is looking to rebuild his tariffs wall after the Supreme Court struck down earlier levies. Now, the language from Beijing is a familiar one and something that we have seen a lot of in the past. At the end of the day, there is a difference between threatening retaliation and actually delivering it. On the latter, I'd actually pay more attention on how Beijing might look to hit back through other avenues.

title: German consumer confidence remains in the doldrums heading into December
body: Germany December GfK consumer confidence -30.2 vs -29.9 expected Prior -30.8; revised to -30.9 German consumer sentiment edged up heading into December but continues to remain subdued as a whole, according to the latest GfK/NIM survey. The breakdown shows that economic expectations falling to -1.6 from 2.1 while price expectations also nudged up a little to 2.8 from 1.0 previously. THe only real bright spot is that income expectations improved a little to -13.9 from -15.7 before this. But at the balance, the report is still suggesting that consumer confidence remains in the dumps. GfK/NIM even noted that the index was "more or less stagnating at a low level" and that doesn't bode well ahead of the Christmas shopping season. If anything else, this does provide some suggestion to the ECB that the euro area's largest economy is still not exactly recovering all too well despite the more resilient showing in the first half of the year. The second half of the year looks to be one of consolidating and stagnating momentum, which isn't the most ideal situation as inflation pressures remain strong. For now, policymakers may still get away with another rate hike, or perhaps even two, but the challenge will grow to be greater next year amid higher stagflationary risks potentially. title: BOJ policymaker Tamura hints at faster rate hikes, keeps December in focus
body: A 50 bps rate hike by the BOJ? Now, wouldn't that be something? We're hearing more comments from BOJ policymaker Tamura today and he is not shying away about talking up the prospect of more aggressive rate hikes by the central bank. His latest remarks: I do have an image in mind of raising interest rates once every few months If inflation risks materialise, BOJ may need to speed up pace of rate hikes or even deliver a 50 bps rate hike Stock, asset price moves are among factors we will look at in measuring financial conditions Would look to decide policy by looking at the data, as well as economic, financial developments leading up to December meeting Before we get too carried away by the headlines though, let's remember who we're dealing with here. Tamura has been one of the leading hawks at the BOJ since joining the central bank in July 2022. So, none of this is particularly out of character. As such, the more interesting question is whether how other policymakers are feeling and if they are viewing things the same way as Tamura is. For now, there's no real suggestion of any overly hawkish leanings along the same lines at least. For the most part, the BOJ has already acknowledged that underlying inflation has broadly reached its 2% target. However, they're not explicitly taking any steps or setting out a position to pre-commit to a rate hike for December and also for next year. As things stand, traders are pricing in roughly 70% odds of a 25 bps rate hike in December.

title: Heads up: Thanksgiving holiday leaves dip buyers in limbo
body: The turkey couldn't have come at a more awkward time for Wall Street, could it? Just as things were starting to get interesting again after yesterday's impressive recovery, US traders are now off to enjoy their Thanksgiving break. As a reminder, US stock and bond markets will be closed today in observance of Thanksgiving. And even though trading resumes tomorrow, Wall Street will only be open until 1800 GMT (1pm ET) while the bond market will wrap things up at 1900 GMT (2pm ET). But in reality, many market participants will already have one foot out the door until Monday. So, one can reasonably expect thinner liquidity conditions across broader markets over the next two days - especially during US trading hours. That being said, let's not mistake a lack of liquidity for a lack of volatility. With fewer buyers and sellers around, it takes considerably less money to move markets. Any relatively modest order size or unexpected headlines could make for some rather exaggerated moves in currencies, gold and stock futures. And given how fragile the market sentiment is looking this week, I'd be particularly wary of reading too much into any technical breakouts or breakdowns during the coming two days. As much as the turnaround yesterday was quite encouraging, the real test for dip buyers will be whether they can continue to build on that momentum once the usual crowd returns next week.

title: ES - 2026-11-26 - Jan Camenisch, Julien Donnet, Simon Lavater and Thomas Moser: Wholesale CBDC on public permissionless blockchains: Challenges, trade-offs, and design choices
body: Stablecoins are the dominant settlement asset on public permissionless blockchains, but as private money they expose users to credit and liquidity risk and can trade away from par. Wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) offers settlement in central bank money, free of credit risk, but has so far been implemented only on permissioned platforms. This paper examines the feasibility of issuing wCBDC on public permissionless blockchains, where tokenized financial activity is growing. It does not advocate such a step. Rather, it analyzes the safeguards such a design would require, focusing on direct Layer-1 issuance as the case in which the central bank has the least control over the underlying infrastructure. The analysis shows that central bank control differs across three levels. At the asset level, smart-contract rules allow the central bank to retain control over the monetary instrument. At the application level, interaction with third-party smart contracts enables composability but complicates eligibility controls and orderly exit. At the network level, transaction inclusion, protocol evolution and service continuity lie outside central bank control and can be fully recovered only through governed components that constrain permissionless interaction. The design choice is therefore a spectrum rather than a binary one. Credible exit and migration arrangements are essential.
